extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers/directors, and students learning stage improvisation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for improvisers, teachers and directors on diagnosing performer problems, running workshops, side-coaching, directing formats (Micetro vs Gorilla) and performer mental practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wimp (slowness/lack of conviction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improviser lacks the conviction that their ideas are worthwhile, believes choices must be carefully considered, imagines others' brains work faster, and acts slowly or freezes after a strong opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: sees improvisation as stressful and may be miserable doing it; version of the “quiet” tendency under 'Control'. Cure: place improviser in a safe, supportive atmosphere and push them to act quickly with exercises demanding spontaneity (Standing Wave, New Choice, Overconfessing, Master/Servant Dubbing). Don't cosset them; make them do things they claim they can't and show them they can; don't punish failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joker (compulsive gagging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improviser has a compulsion to be funny all the time, editorializing rather than emoting, forcing absurdity, steering rapidly towards taboo material, and preferring gags over story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: believes it's their responsibility to make the scene funny above all, may panic and fall back on gagging. Cure: teacher must have zero tolerance for unnecessary gagging and help improviser find success via other avenues (commit to characters, play slow/awkward scenes to show alternative success). Use games requiring close observation/instant reacting; try 'It’s Tuesday' for big reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes Man (over-acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improviser blandly accepts any idea, rarely plays unpleasant characters, finds solutions that prevent middles of stories from taking off; charming but unable to create trouble or be an effective antagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: quickly accepts offers but is uncomfortable with dramatic situations; in life may be a people-pleaser. Cure: feedback games such as The King Game, “Nope!” and The Removalists to remind them dramatic offers please partners/audiences; let them fail to solve a problem (e.g., stolen watch) so the scene generates interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shiner (attention-seeking/controlling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improviser strives to be the focus of attention, blocks offers that don't make them the hero, often high-status and unbothered by what happens; can subtly wrap stories around themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: driven by ego or fear; Teﬂon Shiner offers slide off them. Cure: remind improvisers that best work comes from collaboration; encourage treating perceived-inferior improvisers as equals. If they reject collaboration, suggest alternative careers (solo writer, stand-up). Teachers/directors are especially prone to this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random (excessive unusual offers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improviser makes very unusual offers frequently; if not justified/treated as unusual, story coherence is lost or audience interest fades because character unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: may be genuinely unusual or straining for effect—'that’s not good enough'. Cure: require truthful responses to partners' offers; teach sparing use of peculiar offers. Challenge them with Boring or Truthful scenes (panel of judges throw them off if they make interesting/false offers) to show audience interest in ordinary situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard workers (overthinking/overcontrolling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improviser can do good work but operates at slower pace, wears a frown, justifies destructive choices with rules, hates losing, and makes displeasure known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: may or may not have high self-opinion; believes harder work equals better output. Cure: surround with happy, playful people and reward enthusiasm rather than technique. Use intuitive games like Word At A Time, praise spirited failures; emphasize improv as joyous creativity, not fierce concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume everyone can improvise (teaching stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers begin with the assumption that everybody can improvise despite varying acting chops, physical flexibility or speech defects; identify barriers and gently remove them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagnostics to figure out what’s stopping a student and address those specific obstacles; combine this assumption with targeted exercises and side-coaching to speed learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-coaching (instant corrective instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shout out instructions the improvisers can follow immediately so they can correct errors while still experiencing the successful version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many teachers avoid side-coaching but it points out errors 'on the horizon' and corrects them instantly. Students not used to it can learn to accept it; more experienced students need less side-coaching. Alternative strategies: wait for natural scene end and volunteer notes, or freeze action and discuss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere reviewing—teach to make work better
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not run workshops as simple review sessions where teacher praises success or moves on; the teacher's role is to create a safe atmosphere to criticize the work and make it better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be of the work not the person. Offering only 'That wasn't very good' and moving on is reviewing, not teaching. Create safe/happy atmosphere so criticism can be fearless and productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer useful solutions not 'what you could have done'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the post-show line 'What you could have done there is...' as it is the most useless direction; instead offer a range of productive options so improvisers don't feel there is one right answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving solutions, present multiple productive options to avoid implying a single correct fix and to encourage exploration rather than paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshops must be active learning (doing, not lecturing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation is primarily learned by doing; teachers should offer more than turns—provide exercises, side-coaching and concrete instruction rather than just letting people have lots of turns (which becomes a lecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waiting until the end for notes can make workshops depressing. Freeze-and-discuss increases talk-to-action ratio; balance critique with immediate correction and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director: Speak up (intervene when needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the scene is going badly, the director must say something and intervene; responsibility for improving the work is on the director's shoulders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitching in shares the pain and signals leadership; sitting back with folded arms undermines trust and the chance to improve the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director: Shut up (be unobtrusive when show is good)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the show is going well, the director should be seen and not heard; don't pad your part or call attention to yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for contributions that the audience forgets; avoid interventions that pull the audience out of the story. See Gorilla vs Micetro directing distinctions for when director presence should be more or less visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director: Be bold (push story forward and deliver promises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Push the story into the future and deliver the promises improvisers have made (e.g., cut to honeymoon after a proposal, exploit suggested-dangerous objects safely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to get the story to dark/risky/taboo places by suggestion rather than enactment; you don't have to perform taboo actions—suggest them. Use boldness to liven dull stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director: Be obvious (trust first instincts but respect context)
rubrics_metrics.description: An experienced director's sense of 'obvious' tends to work; say the first obvious interventions—but always consider existing context and avoid substituting your obvious for the improvisers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improvisers have established a different context, don't force a U-turn. If you lack experience, someone else should be directing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director: Get it right (have experience and temperament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you have the experience and temperament to direct; avoid being asleep at the wheel, yanking players like puppets, panicking, or imposing pet topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directing poorly can be worse than not directing; know your limits and step aside if you cannot improve the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director: Make mistakes (permission to fail and learn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors should accept that they will make mistakes; learning to direct requires doing it and screwing up occasionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note they typically screw up about one scene every four shows; acknowledge errors calmly and use them as learning opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micetro vs Gorilla directing (different purposes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Micetro directing exists to make the scene more successful; Gorilla directing exists to draw attention to the directing process (the 'second story').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micetro directing should be learned first; Gorilla directing can be explored later as it often makes scenes worse in entertaining ways (crash-and-burn). In Gorilla Theatre, directors take turns and audience punishes/rewards them; this allows gags to be incorporated safely and supports the two-story dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to be directed (accept and execute instructions immediately)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a director gives an instruction or a line, do it immediately and word for word; don't wait, contemplate, paraphrase, or rewrite it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewriting directed lines calls attention to the direction and undermines the laugh or moment. If you and the director are in sync, that's good; if the director is padding, don't complain onstage—consider replacing them offstage. Three possible cases when director gives something you were about to do: everyone knew, same idea occurred, or director is padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director should genuinely improve work (don't be a perpetual screwer-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you take the role of director, you must genuinely make the work better; otherwise there's no point in having a sideline director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid permanent presence that perpetually screws the work up. Directors should be judged by whether their interventions help the scene; if not, they should be replaced or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer mental practice: let go of failures and reinforce successes
rubrics_metrics.description: Close your eyes, replay an awful moment and let it go; then play back moments when you 'really had it' to create a 'Greatest Hits Tape' to reinforce talent and build confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mental exercise often (before auditions/opening nights) to create positive memory reinforcement and counter the human tendency to obsess over failures. Teachers recommend students build such tapes over a course (e.g., RADA Summer School) to create lifelong confidence and souvenirs.
